name: Visual Question Answering Datasets Review
description: A comprehensive review of Visual Question Answering (VQA) datasets, algorithms, and evaluation metrics. The paper examines multiple VQA datasets including DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA), FM-IQA, Visual7W, Visual Genome, and SHAPES. It critically analyzes dataset construction, biases, limitations, and proposes recommendations for future VQA research.
creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan
citeAs: Kafle, K., & Kanan, C. (2017). Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges. arXiv preprint arXiv:1610.01465v4.
rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets were created using different collection methods. DAQUAR used images from NYU-DepthV2 Dataset with manual question generation. COCO-QA used an NLP algorithm to automatically derive QA pairs from COCO image captions. The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA) employed Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions by asking them to 'Stump a smart robot', with separate workers providing answers. SYNTH-VQA used synthetic cartoon images with manually generated questions. FM-IQA collected questions and answers in Chinese with English translations. Visual Genome used two methods: free-form questions and region-specific prompting where annotators were prompted to ask questions about specific image regions. Visual7W is a subset of Visual Genome.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Surveys
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were sourced from multiple datasets: NYU-DepthV2 Dataset (DAQUAR), Microsoft Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset containing 328,000 images with 91 common object categories and over 2 million labeled instances (COCO-QA, COCO-VQA, FM-IQA, Visual Genome, Visual7W), synthetic cartoon images (SYNTH-VQA with 50,000 synthetic scenes made from over 100 different objects, 30 animal models, and 20 human cartoon models), and Flickr100M (Visual Genome, Visual7W).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, longer sentences were broken into smaller chunks for processing by the NLP algorithm. For FDA model, object labels and bounding boxes were obtained from COCO annotations during training, and during testing, labels were obtained by classifying each bounding box using ResNet. For Visual Genome, semantic segmentation was used to identify objects and their positions in images.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: DAQUAR: Manual question generation. COCO-QA: Automatic generation using NLP algorithm from image captions. The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA): Amazon Mechanical Turk workers generated 3 questions per image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot', with 10 answers per question collected from separate workers. SYNTH-VQA: 3 questions per scene with 10 ground truth answers per question. FM-IQA: Human generated answers and questions, originally in Chinese with English translations. Visual Genome: Average of 17 QA pairs per image using free-form method and region-specific prompting. Visual7W: Subset of Visual Genome with 'telling' questions (text-based answers) and 'pointing' questions (bounding box selection). DAQUAR-consensus: Average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For The VQA Dataset, inter-human agreement is about 83.3%. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% of these questions having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of the 'yes/no' answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. The VQA Dataset uses a consensus-based evaluation metric where if an algorithm agrees with three or more annotators, it is awarded a full score. For Visual7W, plausible multiple-choice answers are collected by prompting annotators to answer questions without seeing the image.
rai:annotationsPerItem: DAQUAR: 1 answer per question initially, DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 answers per question. COCO-QA: 1 answer per question. The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA): 10 answers per question. Visual Genome: average of 17 QA pairs per image. Visual7W: multiple-choice format with 4 possible answers.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm for COCO-QA question generation from captions. ResNet for object classification in bounding boxes (FDA model). Semantic segmentation tools for object identification. Edge Boxes for generating bounding box region proposals.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: SYNTH-VQA human cartoon models contain variations in age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses potential applications for VQA as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. VQA could improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content and be used for image retrieval without using image meta-data or tags.
rai:dataBiases: Multiple significant biases are identified across datasets. COCO-VQA contains many subjective, opinion-seeking questions without single objective answers. Yes/no answers span about 38% of all questions, with almost 59% answered with 'yes'. Language biases allow relatively simple image-blind algorithms to achieve 49.6% accuracy using questions alone. COCO-QA has only four kinds of questions limited to caption content. Questions that require image content are often easy to answer due to strong language biases. For COCO-VQA, answering 'yes' to all yes/no questions yields 71% accuracy instead of expected 50%. Dataset contains easily exploitable biases in question and answer distributions. Questions about drapes may cause algorithms to look at beds rather than windows due to bedroom context bias. The paper demonstrates that the MCB-ensemble model achieved only 47% accuracy on a balanced yes/no dataset about person presence, contrasting with 83% on COCO-VQA yes/no questions, indicating severe training bias. Question phrasing strongly biases answers, with MCB-ensemble achieving 33.6% for 'What are they doing?', 78% for 'What are they playing?', and 86.4% for 'What sport are they playing?' on the same images.
rai:dataLimitations: DAQUAR is too small to successfully train and evaluate complex models, contains exclusively indoor scenes constraining question variety, and has significant clutter with extreme lighting conditions making questions difficult (humans achieve only 50.2% accuracy). COCO-QA has awkwardly phrased questions with grammatical errors due to NLP algorithm flaws, and is limited to four question types. The VQA Dataset contains subjective questions lacking single objective answers, many questions seeking explanations or verbose descriptions, and unreliability of human annotators. FM-IQA allows full sentence answers making automatic evaluation intractable, requiring expensive human judges. Visual Genome's long-tailed answer distribution (1000 most frequent answers cover only 65% vs 82% for COCO-VQA) makes open-ended evaluation challenging. Answer diversity may artificially stem from phrasing variations. Multiple-choice evaluation can be reduced to determining correct answers rather than actually answering questions. Current datasets are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has 'solved' VQA. Algorithms do not have enough data for training and evaluation. Bias in datasets severely limits ability to properly train and assess VQA algorithms. Questions that require image content are often relatively easy to answer. Harder questions like 'Why' questions are comparatively rare, making it difficult to evaluate performance on complex reasoning. A system improving accuracy on 'Is' and 'Are' questions by 15% increases overall accuracy by 5%, while same increase on 'Why' and 'Where' questions only increases accuracy by 0.6%.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation. The datasets are used to train and evaluate VQA algorithms that answer text-based questions about images. Applications include: aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, improving human-computer interaction, image retrieval without meta-data or tags, and as a component of Visual Turing Test for image understanding. The paper recommends that future datasets should evaluate different kinds of questions individually using mean per-question type performance rather than standard accuracy, so each question type would not have equal weight.
